title: When Foundation Models are One-Liners: Limitations and Future Directions for Time Series Anomaly Detection
claim: Both forecasting and reconstruction foundation models can be applied to anomaly detection through the same normalize, predict, de-normalize, score, and pad steps.
layout: Time series on top, two parallel horizontal pipeline rows below, left-to-right, math in boxes
description: A long black periodic time series, similar to an ECG, runs across the top. A dashed rounded box highlights one window, T_{i,i+w-1}. A short stretch in the middle is highlighted in red as an anomaly. Two dashed arrows lead from the window to two parallel horizontal rows, labeled Forecasting-based and Reconstruction-based. Each row has three tall boxes: yellow Normalize, pink F(forecast) or F(reconstruct), and yellow De-Normalize. Arrows then lead to a small white box holding the forecast x-hat or the reconstruction T-hat, then to a blue rounded box with the anomaly-score formula, squared error or MSE. A boxed padding rule sits at the far right of each row. Column labels run along the bottom: TSFM architecture, Forecast/reconstruction, Compute anomaly score, Padding. The eye goes first to the red anomaly and the colored blocks.
caption: Application of TSFMs on TSAD. Given time series subsequence Ti,i+w−1, a forecastingbased TSFM predicts the next observation ˆxi+w and computes the anomaly score as the squared error with xi+w. A reconstruction-based TSFM produces reconstruction ˆTi,i+w−1 of the complete subsequence Ti,i+w−1 and computes the anomaly score as the mean squared error across all observations in the subsequence.
abstract: Recent efforts have extended the foundation model paradigm from natural language to time series, raising expectations that pre-trained time-series foundation models generalize well across downstream tasks. In this work, we focus on time-series anomaly detection, in which time-series foundation models detect anomalies based on the reconstruction or forecasting error. Specifically, we critically examine the performance of five popular families of time-series foundation models: MOMENT, Chronos, TimesFM, Time-MoE, and TSPulse. We find that for each model family using varying model sizes and context window lengths, anomaly detection performance does not significantly differ to simple one-liner baselines: moving-window variance and squared-difference. These findings suggest that the key assumptions underlying reconstruction-based and forecasting-based methodologies for time-series anomaly detection are not satisfied for time-series foundation models: anomalies are not consistently harder to reconstruct or forecast. The results suggest that current approaches for leveraging foundation models in anomaly detection are insufficient. Building upon our insights, we propose alternative directions to effectively detect anomalies using foundation models, thereby unlocking their full potential for time-series anomaly detection.
